7.type_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is the University of Arkansas's top pick for most soils across the belt, and that covers the Ozark uplands: cultivars like Premier and Powderblue are the dependable default. Low-chill southern highbush (Emerald, Jewel) is a genuine alternative on the more acidic, well-drained soils some upland gardens have, and both types are already on this crop's canonical variety list. Northern highbush is heat-stressed here and is not recommended. Rabbiteye's real winter, unlike the mild Deep South, means it drops its leaves and rests fully dormant rather than holding foliage nearly year round.

Here in the Ozark uplands' real winter, rabbiteye loses its leaves and rests like a typical fruit bush, unlike in the much milder Deep South.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye blooms later than highbush and usually escapes spring freezes here; a warm late-winter spell can occasionally push bloom early in a mild year.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent deciduous shrub in the Ozark uplands' real winter, planted once and productive for decades. It rests dormant and leafless through winter, then blooms in spring, sets fruit, and ripens across early summer. After leaf drop, prune late in the dormant season, just before bud break. It needs a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby to cross pollinate and set a crop; the belt's abundant winter chill (roughly 900 to 1,300 hours, far more than rabbiteye's 350 to 600 hour need) is never the limiting factor here.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years. Here it loses its leaves and rests over winter like a typical fruit bush. It flowers in spring and ripens berries by early summer. Plant a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby so the two can pollinate each other and make fruit.

8.type_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is the University of Arkansas's top pick for most soils, and that holds across the lowland South, with Premier, Powderblue, and Tifblue among the dependable cultivars. On the lowland South's more acidic, well-drained soils, low-chill southern highbush (Emerald, Jewel) is a strong second choice and can ripen a bit earlier than rabbiteye. Both types are already on this crop's canonical variety list; rabbiteye remains the broader, more soil-forgiving default across the belt, while northern highbush is too heat-stressed to recommend here.
8.type_note_beginner: Rabbiteye, such as Premier or Tifblue, is the University of Arkansas's top recommendation for most soils here. If your soil is especially acidic and well drained, low-chill southern highbush like Emerald or Jewel is also a strong choice and can ripen a bit earlier. Either way, this belt's real winter means the bush loses its leaves and rests each year.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye blooms early here and can occasionally meet a late-winter freeze in a mild year; later-blooming cultivars are the safer bet.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent deciduous shrub on the lowland South too; the region's real winter, milder than the Ozark uplands' but still a genuine cold season, means it drops its leaves and rests dormant each year rather than holding foliage. It blooms early, in March, and ripens from June into mid-July. Prune late in the dormant season, just before bud break, and plant a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby for cross pollination. Abundant regional chill (roughly 900 to 1,300 hours a year, far more than rabbiteye needs) is never the limiting factor.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry on the lowland South is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years. It loses its leaves and rests over winter, flowers early in spring, and ripens berries from June into mid-July. Plant a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby so the two can pollinate each other.

blueberry.region_notes_beginner: The Mid-South is real blueberry country. Rabbiteye, such as Premier and Powderblue, is the type the University of Arkansas recommends for most home gardens here. Low-chill southern highbush like Emerald or Jewel is a good second option where the soil is naturally acidic and well drained. Unlike the Deep South, our real winter means the bush loses its leaves and rests each year. Plant in early spring, expect flowers in late winter to spring, and pick berries from June into midsummer. Always plant two different rabbiteye varieties together so they can pollinate each other.
blueberry.region_notes_seasoned: The Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands are genuine blueberry country. The University of Arkansas recommends rabbiteye (Premier, Powderblue, Brightwell, Tifblue) as the best all-around choice for most soils across the belt, with low-chill southern highbush (Emerald, Jewel) a strong option where the soil is naturally acidic and well drained. Northern highbush struggles in the region's summer heat and is not the pick here. Unlike se_gulf's mild winter, this belt's real winter in both zones means rabbiteye is grown here as a fully deciduous shrub, dropping its leaves and resting dormant rather than holding foliage year round. Chill is never the limiting factor: the belt banks roughly 900 to 1,300 hours a year against rabbiteye's roughly 350 to 600 hour requirement. Plant at least two different rabbiteye cultivars for cross pollination, and prune in the dormant season just before bud break.

7.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) blackberry is the type to grow across the Ozark uplands, and it is squarely at home here: the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program developed most of the state's standard cultivars. Thornless erect and semi-erect types (Ouachita, Navaho, Apache) are the easiest to pick and manage, and chill is never a limiter, since even the highest-chill University of Arkansas releases (about 800 to 900 hours) are cleared many times over by the uplands' winter.
7.type_note_beginner: Grow a summer-bearing blackberry, ideally a thornless upright University of Arkansas type like Ouachita or Navaho, easy to pick and manage. Winters here are plenty cold for it.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blackberries bloom in May here, well after the last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk. Winter cold is not a limiting factor for these cultivars.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Blackberry is a deciduous cane fruit here: the canes drop their leaves and rest through the Ozark uplands winter, banking far more chill than these cultivars need, while the perennial crown and roots live for 15 to 20 years and each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Set dormant bare-root canes from winter into early spring, trellis for support, and prune out the spent fruited canes each dormant season. Watch for rosette (double blossom) and favor resistant cultivars.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your blackberry patch is permanent, even though each cane only lives two years: it grows one season, fruits the next, then dies while new canes take over. Plant dormant canes in winter or early spring, give upright types a simple trellis, and cut out the old fruited canes each winter.

8.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing thornless erect blackberries thrive on the lowland South; the University of Arkansas notes blackberries are adapted to all regions of Arkansas, and its fruit breeding program released the standard cultivars grown here. Ouachita, Navaho, and Apache all fruit heavily from late spring into summer. The main disease to watch is rosette (double blossom); scout at bloom and favor resistant cultivars.
8.type_note_beginner: The lowland South grows thornless upright University of Arkansas blackberries like Ouachita and Navaho very well, with a heavy crop from late spring into summer. Watch for rosette disease and pick resistant kinds.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blackberries bloom in mid-spring here, comfortably behind the last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Blackberry is a deciduous cane fruit on the lowland South too: the canes rest through the region's real (if milder than the Ozark uplands') winter, while the perennial crown lives 15 to 20 years and each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Set dormant bare-root canes over winter, trellis for support, and prune out spent fruited canes each dormant season. This is excellent blackberry country: warm, humid summers ripen a heavy crop, and chill is never a limiter.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your blackberry patch on the lowland South is permanent, even though each cane lives only two years. Plant dormant canes over winter, give upright types a trellis, and cut out old fruited canes each winter. This is genuinely great blackberry country.

blackberry.region_notes_beginner: The Mid-South is prime blackberry country, and Arkansas is its home turf. The University of Arkansas fruit breeding program developed most of the thornless upright cultivars grown across the state, and blackberries thrive in both the Ozark uplands and the lowland South, fruiting heavily from late spring into summer. Plant dormant canes over winter into early spring, give them a simple trellis, watch for rosette disease, and cut out the old fruited canes each year. Winters here are far more than cold enough, so chill is never something to worry about.
blackberry.region_notes_seasoned: Blackberry is the Mid-South's signature home-garden fruit, and both zones are excellent for it. The University of Arkansas's FSA6105 (Blackberry Production in the Home Garden) states plainly that blackberries are adapted to all regions of Arkansas, and the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program bred the standard cultivars grown here: thornless erect summer-bearing types (Ouachita, Navaho, Apache), the thorny Kiowa, and the Prime-Ark primocane series. The recommended summer-bearing types fruit on second-year (floricane) canes, with the first crop the year after the planting is established. Chill is a complete non-factor: the belt banks roughly 900 to 1,300 hours a year, clearing the entire University of Arkansas cultivar range (about 200 hours for Kiowa up to 800 to 900 for Apache and Navaho) many times over. The lowland South ripens a few weeks ahead of the Ozark uplands. Plant dormant bare-root canes from winter into early spring, trellis for support, scout for rosette (double blossom) at bloom and favor resistant cultivars, and prune out spent fruited canes each dormant season.

7.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) red raspberry is the type to grow in the Ozark uplands, giving one concentrated early-summer crop on year-old canes. This zone's cooler upland climate is genuinely raspberry-friendly by regional standards; well-drained soil matters, since raspberries are prone to Phytophthora root rot in heavy or wet ground.
7.type_note_beginner: Grow a summer-bearing red raspberry here for one big early-summer crop on year-old canes. Give it soil that drains well, since raspberries are prone to root rot in heavy, wet ground.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Raspberries bloom in May, well after the last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk. Winter cold is not a limiting factor.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit here: the canes drop their leaves and rest through the Ozark uplands winter, banking far more chill than needed, while the perennial crown lives a decade or more and each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. Set dormant bare-root canes over winter into early spring, plant on a raised bed or well-drained site to guard against Phytophthora root rot, trellis, and prune out spent fruited canes and thin new ones each dormant season.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry patch comes back every year, even though each cane only lives two seasons. Plant dormant canes in winter or early spring on a raised, well-drained bed, since wet soil invites root rot. Give the canes a trellis and cut out the old fruited ones each winter.

8.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing red raspberry can be grown on the lowland South, but this is the more marginal end of the belt for this crop: the lowland South's greater summer heat and humidity raise the risk of Phytophthora root rot and general decline more than in the cooler Ozark uplands. Plant on a raised bed with excellent drainage, choose a site with some afternoon shade if summers run hot, and treat plantings as shorter-lived here than farther inland.
8.type_note_beginner: Raspberries can grow on the lowland South, but the heat and humidity make this the harder part of the region for them. Plant on a raised, well-drained bed, give afternoon shade if you can, and expect the planting to need renewing sooner than in cooler spots.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Raspberries bloom in mid-spring here, comfortably behind the last frost, so spring frost on open bloom is a low risk. Summer heat and humidity are the bigger everyday concern.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Raspberry is a deciduous cane fruit on the lowland South too, resting through the region's milder winter before growing and fruiting each summer. The real challenge here is heat and humidity rather than cold: well-drained, raised planting sites are essential to hold off Phytophthora root rot, and afternoon shade helps in the hottest microclimates. Set dormant canes over winter, trellis, and prune out spent fruited canes each dormant season; expect this to be a more marginal, shorter-lived planting than in the cooler Ozark uplands.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry patch on the lowland South rests through our milder winter and grows each summer, but heat and humidity are real challenges here, more so than in the cooler Ozark uplands. Plant on a raised, well-drained bed, consider afternoon shade, and expect it to need replacing sooner than farther inland.

raspberry.region_notes_beginner: Raspberries do well in the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7), giving one big early-summer crop on year-old canes. On the warmer lowland South (zone 8), they can still be grown, but heat and humidity make it more of a challenge, so plant on a raised, well-drained bed and consider some afternoon shade. Give canes a trellis, plant on well-drained ground everywhere to avoid root rot, and cut out old fruited canes each winter.
raspberry.region_notes_seasoned: Raspberries genuinely favor the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7) over the warmer, more humid lowland South (zone 8) in this belt: standard summer-bearing red cultivars (Boyne, Nova, Latham, Killarney) crop reliably in zone 7's cooler upland climate, while zone 8 is more marginal, with summer heat and humidity raising the risk of Phytophthora root rot and general plant decline. Well-drained, raised planting sites matter everywhere, more so on the lowland South, where afternoon shade and shorter planting life expectancy are honest expectations rather than corrections. Chill (roughly 700 to 800 hours) is never a limiting factor in either zone.

7.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the type to grow here, chosen by cultivar rather than climate. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and thrives in the moist soils common across the Ozark uplands; the only real rule is to plant two different cultivars for cross pollination.
7.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry, the common type. It loves moist soil and our winters are more than cold enough for it. Just plant two different varieties near each other for a good crop.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in early summer, well after spring frost, so frost on bloom is rarely a concern here.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent, very cold-hardy deciduous shrub here, planted once and renewed in place for many years. It rests bare and dormant through winter, leafs out and grows fast in spring, blooms in early summer, and ripens dark berry clusters in late summer. Renew the oldest canes in late winter, and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set. This native, adaptable shrub asks for little beyond the moisture the Ozark uplands already supplies.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry is a long-lived, very cold-hardy bush you plant once and keep for years. It loses its leaves and rests in winter, grows fast in spring, flowers in early summer, and ripens dark berries in late summer. Prune the oldest stems in late winter, and plant two different varieties for a good crop.

8.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry grows and fruits readily on the lowland South too; there is no separate warm-climate type as there is for blueberry. It wants steady moisture, which the lowland South's water table and rainfall usually supply. Plant two different cultivars for cross pollination.
8.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry here too, the same common type. It likes plenty of moisture, which the lowland South generally has. Plant two different varieties near each other for a good crop.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in late spring here, well after the last frost, so frost on bloom is rarely a concern.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent deciduous shrub on the lowland South as well, planted once and kept for years, though the region's milder winter means it rests only briefly compared to the Ozark uplands. It blooms in late spring, ripens earlier than upland plantings, from July into August, and is renewed by pruning out the oldest canes in late winter. Plant two different cultivars for good fruit set, and keep it well watered through the summer heat.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry on the lowland South is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years. It rests only briefly over our milder winter, flowers in late spring, and ripens earlier than upland plantings, from July into August. Prune old stems in late winter and plant two different varieties for a good crop.

elderberry.region_notes_beginner: Elderberry is an easy, native-range shrub across the Mid-South. It loves moisture, which this region generally provides, and our winters are more than cold enough for it. Plant in spring, expect flowers from late spring into early summer, and pick dark berries in mid to late summer. Always plant two different varieties together so they can pollinate each other.
elderberry.region_notes_seasoned: Elderberry is native to the Mid-South and genuinely easy here in both zones: American elderberry is exceptionally cold-hardy (chill, about 400 hours, is never a limiter against a belt that banks far more than it needs), thrives in the moist soils common to both the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands, and needs only cultivar diversity, not climate correction, to fruit well. The lowland South's milder winter and earlier spring bring bloom and harvest a few weeks ahead of the Ozark uplands. Plant two different cultivars for cross pollination, keep it well watered through summer heat, and renew the oldest canes each late winter.

strawberry.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked; the crowns are dormant stock, so there is no need to wait out frost danger (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension home garden matted-row guidance).

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: On an established matted-row bed, June-bearing plants begin flowering in the weeks after the last frost; open blossoms are frost-sensitive (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: June-bearing strawberries ripen roughly six weeks after the last frost in the Ozark uplands' matted-row system (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: The June-bearing flush runs about four weeks. Renovate the matted row within two weeks of the last picking: mow the leaves above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: the University of Arkansas's plasticulture system, developed for and widely used across the NC Delta Lowlands and Ozark Uplands, sets plug transplants in mid-September through early October on raised, plastic-mulched beds with drip irrigation. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by the fall establishment season, not anchored to the last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Plants establish through fall, overwinter under row covers as small crowns, then bloom in spring as day length and temperature increase (the University of Arkansas plasticulture guidance).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins in late April in the plasticulture system, several weeks ahead of a matted-row planting, one of the system's main advantages (the University of Arkansas).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Harvest runs into early June, after which the planting is turned under before summer heat and disease pressure build; fresh plugs are set again the following fall (the University of Arkansas plasticulture guidance, the annual-hill system).

strawberry.plantings_provenance: Region fill (Task 7, Claude Code lane, 2026-07-20). The Mid-South genuinely runs BOTH strawberry systems, differentiated honestly by zone rather than picking one for the whole region: zone 7 (Ozark uplands/VA, cooler, the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension-documented) uses the traditional June-bearing perennial matted row, the same shape this crop's own northern_tier cells use, with plant_out/bloom/harvest_start/harvest_end frost-offset from the real last spring frost. Zone 8 (lowland South/NC, warmer, the University of Arkansas-documented) uses the annual plasticulture (fall plug, raised bed, plastic mulch) system the University of Arkansas pioneered and recommends for this belt's lowland South conditions, an absolute month-resolved fall-plant/spring-harvest/summer-removal cycle, structurally like this crop's own se_gulf annual cells but with the University of Arkansas's own earlier fall planting and spring harvest dates (not LSU's Gulf Coast timing). grown_as differs by zone (perennial z7 / annual z8) using the existing grown_as field exactly as intended for this archetype.

7.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Ozark uplands grows strawberries as a perennial matted-row bed, the traditional home-garden system: plant once and the same bed comes back and fruits for several years. Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. June-bearing types give one concentrated flush in late spring, then send runners to fill the row. Renovate the bed within two weeks of the last harvest: mow the leaves above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Ozark uplands, you plant a strawberry bed once and it comes back and fruits for years. Plant the small dormant crowns in early spring, even if frost is still possible. You get one big batch of berries in late spring, then trim and thin the bed after picking to keep it healthy.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blossoms opening in late April to May can still be caught by a late frost; cover the bed with row cover on a forecast frosty night during bloom to protect the crop.

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The lowland South grows strawberries on the plasticulture (annual-hill) system the University of Arkansas recommends, not a perennial bed: set plug transplants in mid-September through early October on raised, plastic-mulched rows with drip irrigation, let plants establish through fall and overwinter as small crowns, then harvest from late April through early June, several weeks ahead of a matted-row planting. After harvest the planting is turned under, since summer heat and disease pressure make it impractical to carry over, and fresh plugs are set again the following fall.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: On the lowland South, strawberries are grown as a fall-planted crop you replace each year, not a bed that lives for years. Set transplants in September or early October on a raised, plastic-covered row. Pick berries from late April into early June, then pull the plants and start fresh again next fall.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Plants overwinter as small crowns under row covers; open spring blossoms are damaged by a hard freeze, so keep row covers or frost protection on hand for a late cold snap during March and April bloom.

strawberry.region_notes_beginner: The Mid-South grows strawberries two different ways depending on where you are. In the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7), plant a matted-row bed once and it comes back for years, with one big batch of berries in late spring. On the warmer lowland South (zone 8), growers use a plastic-covered raised-row system: plant in fall, pick from late April into early June, then replace the planting each year. Both are real, well-documented ways to grow strawberries here.
strawberry.region_notes_seasoned: The Mid-South genuinely runs both major US strawberry systems, split honestly by zone. The cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7) uses the traditional June-bearing perennial matted row documented by University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension: set dormant crowns about two weeks before the last frost, expect one concentrated harvest flush in late spring, and renovate the bed after picking to keep it productive for several years. The warmer lowland South (zone 8) uses the plasticulture (annual-hill) system the University of Arkansas documents for this climate: fall-set plug transplants on raised, plastic-mulched, drip-irrigated rows establish through fall, overwinter as small crowns, and crop from late April through early June, several weeks earlier than a matted-row bed, before the planting is turned under ahead of summer heat and disease pressure and replaced the next fall.
